titleText.es: Presionaría sobre ellos para intentar arreglarlos, pero no alcanzo. ¿Podemos intentar pasar de la noche al día muy rápido?
titleText.en: I'd press on them to try to unstick them, but I can't reach. Can we try cycling day and night really fast?
titleText.noteEn: The title text extends the screen metaphor: the tiny colored points in the sky behave like stuck or dead pixels that someone might press or refresh.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Todos can stand on its own for a whole masculine or mixed group. With a first-person plural verb, it includes the speaker and naturally becomes “we all” or “all of us” in English.
Visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver, ‘to see.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have seen.’
Bromeado is the completed-action form of bromear, ‘to joke.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have joked.’

cardDefinitions.answerEn: resolution; the amount of pixel detail in an image or display
cardDefinitions.noteEn: For a screen or image, resolución describes how much pixel detail it can show. In other contexts the same word can mean a solution or a formal decision.
Prepara is a present form of preparar for one person or thing. A short word before it can identify the person being prepared.

example.es: El curso te prepara para el examen.
example.en: The course prepares you for the exam.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: for; required after preparar before what someone is prepared for
cardDefinitions.noteEn: After preparar, para introduces the later situation, event, or action that the preparation is meant to handle.
Shock is an English borrowing used unchanged as a masculine noun in Spanish: el shock. Choque, conmoción, or impresión may be preferred depending on the situation.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: to get up; to rise (one informal listener)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Levantar means ‘to lift,’ while levantarse means to get oneself up. In levantarte, the dictionary form levantar has te attached to identify one familiar person as the person getting up.

example.en: You need to get up early.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: one; a certain (before a feminine time word)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Before a time word, una can introduce one unspecified occasion rather than count several things.
Mañana can be the noun ‘morning’ or the time word ‘tomorrow.’ An article or another determiner before it, as in una mañana, marks the noun meaning.
Píxeles is the plural of píxel, one tiny picture element in a digital image or screen.
With pixels, muertos means that the tiny screen elements no longer light or respond correctly, not that living beings have died.

example.es: La pantalla tiene dos píxeles muertos.
example.en: The screen has two dead pixels.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something prepares a person for a later situation?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use preparar, identify the person being prepared, then use para before the later situation or action.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Only preparar changes for the person and time. A short object word such as me, te, lo, la, nos, los, or las goes before a changed form of preparar. A named person instead follows a, the marker Spanish puts before a specific person receiving an action: prepara a Ana. Para then introduces what that person is being prepared for.

example.es: El curso prepara a Ana para el examen.
example.en: The course prepares Ana for the exam.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say ‘dead pixel’—a screen dot that no longer works correctly?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use píxel muerto; for more than one, use píxeles muertos.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: This is the conventional technical expression. Muerto describes píxel, so it changes to muertos when píxel changes to the plural píxeles.

example.es: El monitor tiene un píxel muerto.
example.en: The monitor has a dead pixel.
